what: Kite Realty owns open-air shopping centres in the United States, most of them anchored by a grocery store or a large discount retailer. Tenants pay rent on long leases and cover much of the operating cost of the property.
customers: National and regional retailers - grocers, off-price stores, restaurants, fitness and service businesses - that want locations people visit weekly.
money: Base rent and recoveries from tenants in grocery-anchored and power centres.
Parking, percentage rent, fees and other income from the centres.
moat: Grocery-anchored centres are hard to replicate: zoning, land and the need for a willing grocer limit new supply, and needs-based tenants keep footfall steady even when online shopping grows.
risks: Tenant bankruptcies among weaker retailers leave boxes that take time and capital to re-let.
Higher interest rates raise refinancing costs on $3.1 billion of debt and compete with REIT yields.
Growth is slow by nature: rent rises a few per cent a year.
opportunities: Little new retail space is being built, which gives landlords pricing power on renewals.
Recycling capital from weaker centres into stronger ones can lift the quality of the portfolio over time.
watch: Leasing spreads and occupancy. They show whether tenants are paying more on renewal, which is the only real growth engine in this business.
view: Ignore the P/E of about 15 on Kite Realty: the $340 million of net income includes gains from selling properties, and a REIT’s accounting earnings are distorted by depreciation on buildings that in practice hold their value. The useful measures are funds from operations, occupancy and the rent increases on new and renewed leases. Revenue, which jumped in 2022 when Kite merged with Retail Properties of America, has since grown only from $802 million to $844 million, which is what a stable, mature portfolio looks like.

The case for open-air retail has quietly improved. Almost no new shopping centres have been built for a decade, so the supply of good space has shrunk while the tenants that thrive - grocers, off-price, services, restaurants - want physical locations near where people live. That gives landlords like Kite the upper hand when leases come up, and it is why the sector came through the retail apocalypse narrative in better shape than most people expected.

What the market is pricing in at $24.61 is a steady, bond-like stream with modest growth, and that seems roughly right. The risks are refinancing costs if rates stay high and the occasional tenant bankruptcy; the upside is a few years of strong renewal spreads. This is a fairly priced income holding rather than a mispriced opportunity, and it should be compared against the yield on safer assets before anything else.
bull: Scarce supply keeps renewal spreads high and occupancy near full, lifting cash flow steadily while capital recycling improves the portfolio.
bear: Rates stay high, refinancing eats into cash flow, and a wave of retailer failures leaves vacant boxes that take years to fill.
